sections.html:
• Common name: Cabomba; other names: Fanwort, Carolina water-shield, Fish grass, Green Cabomba, Washington grass, Washington-plant
  • Lighting: high
  • Substrate: any / floating
  • Growth rate: fast
  • Placement: background
  • Size: 20 to 50+ cm
  • Fertilizers: yes
  • CO2: yes
  • Propagation: by cuttings
  • Colour: green (the red form is rarer)

Important: the plant is popular in the hobby but behaves invasively in several European and Asian countries, as well as parts of the USA and Canada. Cabomba caroliniana is banned in certain U.S. states (for example California, Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Vermont and Washington) and is on the list of EU Regulation 1143/2014 on invasive alien species. Make sure it is not banned where you live and do not buy or sell it illegally.

Cabomba is available at local aquarium or pet stores at relatively low prices, usually as a bunch of 5 or more stems held by a rubber band. Choose tall healthy stems with vibrant pale/lime-green or reddish-purple leaves; small roots, flowers and new shoots are signs of good health.

Quarantine and disinfect the plant before adding it, unless it was grown in vitro in an undamaged sealed pot. It can carry parasites, pest snails, predators (dragonfly or damselfly nymphs) and pesticide residues that are extremely poisonous to fish and shrimp.

Cabomba is native to South America and belongs to the family Cabombaceae, which has two genera, Brasenia and Cabomba. It is distributed mainly across the Americas, from South America to the southern United States. It has also spread to Canada (Lake Kasshabog) and other temperate and tropical regions of the Old and New World.

Cabomba caroliniana comes from the southern United States and extends to South America. Cabomba aquatica is common in Brazil, Guyana and Argentina. Cabomba furcata (also known as Cabomba piauhyensis or Red Cabomba) is distributed from Central America to South America.

Cabomba lives in fresh still waters or waters with a slight current: lakes, streams and rivers. In nature it grows primarily in loose substrates and does not root very deeply. Cabomba species are exclusively submersed in their natural habitats; when the water dries out the plant forms only two to three emersed leaves and can survive in that state only for a limited time.
Cabomba suits both small (about 40 litres) and large aquariums. The stem branches strongly and, depending on the species, may reach 2 m or more if not pruned.

Cabomba is often labelled "easy" by the trade, but it needs lots of nutrients and light, and some knowledge to balance a high-tech planted tank. Nutrient limitation of nitrates brings out the real colours. Regular dosing of plant fertiliser is needed.

It grows rapidly, up to 2.5 cm per day in favourable conditions, so regular pruning is needed or it will grow up to the surface. Damaged stems and dead or decomposed leaves can clog the filter and ruin water quality, so remove them together with the trimmings.

Planting: place healthy stems at least 2.5 cm deep in the substrate, after removing the lower two or three pairs of leaves, in bunches of five or six stems. If stems float up, poke them back with tweezers or hold them down with lead weights. Another trick is to put the stem inside a ceramic ring, or leave it floating until roots grow and then anchor it. Floating is also possible: remove the rubber band, disinfect the stems and place them on the surface; adventitious roots will sprout after a while.

Propagation: asexual by fragmentation and sexual via emergent flowers. In the aquarium, take terminal cuttings of about 10–12 cm from mature stems and plant them in the substrate. Cut gently because the stems are fragile. Trimming the top makes the plant bushier.

Common problems:

  • Leaves falling off: usually light or CO2 deficiency.
  • Bottom leaves turning brown: bushy upper leaves block light from reaching them.
  • Fragile: the needles break off easily and make a mess.
  • Melting: it does not tolerate environmental change well.
  • Moving: once planted it dislikes being moved; the thin roots are easily damaged and may rot after replanting.
  • Long aerial roots: it tends to grow many of them.

• Temperature: 20–28 °C is optimal. It does not grow well at lower temperatures, although it will survive. Cabomba furcata prefers slightly warmer water, 23–26 °C.
  • pH: slightly acidic to neutral, 6.0–7.5; the best growth was at pH 6.5 in experiments.
  • Hardness: 3–8 GH, soft to moderately hard. In hard water it melts; at a hard alkaline pH of 8.0 and above it will eventually melt completely.
  • Water flow: it dislikes strong flow, which inhibits growth because debris gets trapped in the fan-shaped leaves.

Light: Cabomba grows best in medium to high light and shows good colour and vigorous shoot growth under high light. It cannot adapt to low light. Even at medium light it will not grow well without CO2 injection, and grows tall and leggy. It likes long photoperiods (at least 10–12 hours per day). At least 30–40 PAR is advised for green species and 40–50 PAR for the red/purple form. If the light is not strong enough, Cabomba does better floating than planted. Raising light without CO2 invites an algae bloom; high-tech tanks must be balanced in light, CO2 and nutrients.

Substrate: the substrate does not matter, because Cabomba absorbs nutrients from the water column.

CO2 and fertilisation: CO2 helps keep plants healthy and triggers faster shoot growth, although the plants can do without it under high light. Regular fertilisation is recommended; Cabomba is hard to grow without it. It is a water-column feeder rather than a root feeder, so it benefits from products such as Seachem Excel. If you keep shrimp, remember that high CO2 and copper (found in most fertilisers) are extremely dangerous to them.

Dense Cabomba in the background is good shelter and hiding spot for fry and small fish, and some fish use it for spawning. Compatible tankmates include peaceful fish (Otocinclus, pygmy corydoras, neon tetras, guppies, cherry barbs, green swordtails, rasboras, platies), shrimp (Neocaridina and Caridina varieties, Amano, ghost, bamboo and vampire shrimp) and snails (ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet, Japanese trapdoor, mystery snails), though some snails may damage the plant.

Avoid voracious plant-eaters such as silver dollars, Oscars and Buenos Aires tetras, which can break the brittle leaves. Crayfish and freshwater crabs may cut or uproot the plant unless it is left floating.

Benefits: suited to jungle-style aquascapes; absorbs nitrate, ammonia and phosphate from the water; competes with algae for nutrients; shelters fish, fry and shrimp; provides biofilm as a first food for fry and shrimplets; oxygenates the water.

It looks much like hornwort (Ceratophyllum demersum). Submersed leaves are thread-shaped, divided into fine segments 25–50 mm long. About eleven Cabomba species are known; few are popular in the trade.

  • Cabomba caroliniana: leaves divided into narrow segments, white flowers with a yellow centre; green, very easy to grow. Var. multipartita is the best form; var. pauciparitta is delicate and of little value; var. pulcherrima has purple-red stems and leaves and tolerates shade.
  • Cabomba aquatica: grows up to about 60 cm; whitish-yellow round flowers with an orange spot at the base.
  • Cabomba furcata (Red Cabomba): grows slowly, is fragile, sensitive to algae and tends to lose its lower leaves; needs intense light and low nitrate to keep bright red to purple colour.

In conclusion, Cabomba tends either to die quickly or to become a weed. Beginners are advised to start with green Cabomba; hornwort is an easier look-alike.
